lessons.title: Lesson text — Morning Walk (p. 8-10)
lessons.notes_html:
Ahmed lives in Quetta. One day, he woke up very early in the morning. The sky was soft and light grey and a cool breeze was blowing. He got out of bed, brushed his teeth and washed his face. Then he put on his tracksuit and joggers. His mother gave him a bottle of water and reminded him to be careful while crossing the road. The night before, Ahmed had told his cousin Zain that he would go for a morning walk. So, early in the morning, Zain came to Ahmed's house. As Ahmed stepped outside, he saw Zain waiting at the gate with a smile. 'Let's go together!' said Zain happily. The road was almost empty. A few men were walking or riding bicycles. They could see tiny drops of dew on the grass and the leaves. Ahmed and Zain talked and laughed as they walked to Jinnah Park, which was just a few minutes away from their home. When they reached the park, they were happy to see green trees and flowers all around. A gardener was watering the trees and plants. The boys removed their shoes and walked on the soft, wet grass. It felt cold and tickled their toes. After walking and playing for about fifteen minutes, they sat under a tree and drank some water. Zain saw a butterfly and tried to chase it. Ahmed laughed and ran after him. They both felt full of energy and very fresh. Soon, it was time to go back. Zain said goodbye to Ahmed at the street corner near their homes and waved with a smile. He turned towards his house, feeling cheerful after the walk. When Ahmed returned

home, his mother had prepared a healthy breakfast of paratha, an egg and a glass of milk. Ahmed washed his hands and had his breakfast. Ahmed had learnt that morning walk is good for health, gives us energy and keeps our mind fresh. He decided to wake up early every day and enjoy a morning walk.

lessons.title: Grammar — Noun: Types of a Noun (p. 15-17)
lessons.notes_html: Noun is the name of a person, place, animal or thing, e.g., Ali, city, cat, pen, etc. 1. Common Nouns: refer to general, non-specific people, places, things, or animals, etc. Examples: teacher, doctor, player, city, park, school, book, table, car. Sentences: (i) The teacher helped the students with their homework. (ii) The city was full of buildings. (iii) We go to school daily. 2. Proper Nouns: the proper names of people, places, or things etc. and are always capitalized. Examples: Mujtaba, Ali, Ziarat, Chiltan, Askri-Park, Book. Sentences: (i) She is going to visit Karachi next summer. (ii) Mujtaba is my elder brother. (iii) I like English Book. 3. Countable Nouns: nouns that can be counted. Examples: apple - apples, cat - cats, book - books. Sentences: (i) Singular: I ate an apple for a snack. (ii) Plural: The cats chased each other around the garden. 4. Uncountable Nouns: nouns that cannot be counted. Examples: water, sugar, rice, love, advice. Sentences: (i) Please pass me a glass of water. (ii) His advice was very helpful. (iii) I like rice. 5. Collective Nouns: refer to groups of people or things as a single entity. Examples: team, family, class, herd, flock, bunch. Sentences: (i) The team celebrated their victory with a party. (ii) I have a small family. (iii) She picked a bunch of flowers from the garden.

lessons.title: Lesson text — My Family (p. 20-21)
lessons.notes_html:
My name is Shazia, and I want to tell you about my wonderful family. We live in a house with a big garden where we play and enjoy on sunny days. There are six people in my family. They are very special people because each one of them makes my life brighter and happier. Firstly, there are my grandparents, Grandma and Grandpa. They are the oldest in our family, but they are also the wisest and kindest. Grandma bakes the most delicious cookies you have ever tasted, and Grandpa tells the stories from when he was a boy. Sometimes, we gather around them, listening to

their tales with great interest. Secondly, let me introduce you to my parents, Mom and Dad. My mom is like a super lady. She is a teacher. She helps other kids learn new things every day. Dad is a doctor; he wears a white coat and helps people feel better when they are sick. Even though they are busy with work, they always make time for me and my sister. We love when they read us bed time stories or play games with us in the evening. Thirdly, let me introduce my little sister, Aisha. She is the youngest in our family. Aisha loves to read story books, and she is always full of energy. Sometimes, we argue, especially when she borrows my toys without asking, but most of the time, we are the best of friends. Finally, it is me. I am Shazia, the eldest sibling. I like to think of myself as the leader of our little group. I enjoy reading books, drawing pictures and going on adventures with my family. Whether we explore the park or bake cookies together, every moment we spend together is special to me.

lessons.title: Oral Communication Skills — Dialogue (p. 25-26)
lessons.notes_html:
Father, mother, daughter and son are talking. Mama: Ahmed, can you tell

us about your school today? Ahmed: Yes, Mama. Today, our teacher asked us to talk about our family. I told everyone that I have a loving family. Baba: That is nice, son. What did you say about us? Ahmed: I said that Baba works in an office and takes care of us. Mama is always busy making delicious food and helping us with our homework. Sara: And what about me? What did you say about me? Ahmed: I said that my little sister, Sara, is very naughty but also very cute. She loves playing with her dolls. Sara: That's true. But you forgot to say that I also love drawing. Mama: Ahmed, that was a great way to describe our family. It's important to listen to others and remember what they like. Baba: Yes, and always respond kindly. Like when Sara reminded you about her drawing, you should say something nice. Ahmed: Oh yes. You are really good at drawing, Sara. Your last drawing of our house was amazing. Sara: Thank you, Ahmed. Mama: That is how we should talk to each other with kindness. Baba: That is right. A good family always listens and respects each other. (Speaking activity - practise the dialogue in pairs in front of the class.)

lessons.title: Sentence Structure — Subject and Predicate (p. 30)
lessons.notes_html: Subject: The subject is who or what the sentence is about. It tells us the main person, animal, thing, or idea that the sentence is talking about. Example: The cat sleeps - 'cat' is the subject. Predicate: The predicate tells us what the subject is doing or what is happening to the subject. It usually includes the verb and other words that give more information about the action. Example: The cat sleeps - 'sleeps' is the predicate. Subject and predicate examples: 1. The dog (Subject) - barks loudly (Predicate). 2. The sun (Subject) - shines brightly in the sky (Predicate).

mcqs.q: What is the subject in a sentence?
options: Who or what the sentence is about
mcqs.why: The subject is who or what the sentence is about, the main person, animal, thing or idea talked about.

mcqs.q: What is the predicate in a sentence?
options: What the subject is doing or what is happening to it
mcqs.why: The predicate tells what the subject is doing or what is happening to the subject, usually including the verb.

mcqs.q: In 'The cat sleeps', what is the subject?
mcqs.why: Cat is the subject in 'The cat sleeps' because the sentence is about the cat, as the example explains.

mcqs.q: In 'The cat sleeps', what is the predicate?
mcqs.why: Sleeps is the predicate in 'The cat sleeps' because it tells what the subject cat is doing.

mcqs.q: In example 1, 'The dog — barks loudly', what is the predicate?

mcqs.q: In example 2, what is the subject?
mcqs.why: The sun is the subject in example 2, and 'shines brightly in the sky' is its predicate part.

mcqs.q: What does the predicate usually include?

mcqs.why: The predicate usually includes the verb and other words that give more information about the action.

mcqs.why: This lesson teaches that a sentence comprises subject and predicate as its two main parts together.

mcqs.q: In 'The sun shines brightly in the sky', what is the predicate?
mcqs.why: Shines brightly in the sky is the predicate telling what the sun does in example 2 of the lesson.

mcqs.q: The subject tells us the main what?
options: Person, animal, thing or idea the sentence talks about
mcqs.why: The subject tells the main person, animal, thing or idea that the sentence is talking about overall.

lessons.title: S + V (Subject and Verb) pattern (p. 30-31)
lessons.notes_html: Subject: The noun or pronoun which performs an action is called subject. Verb: The word that shows an action is called a verb. Examples: 1. Jawad (Subject) - plays (Verb). 2. Ammara (Subject) - cooks (Verb). 3. He (Subject) - writes (Verb). 4. She (Subject) - walks (Verb).

mcqs.q: In the S+V pattern, what is the subject?
options: The noun or pronoun which performs an action
mcqs.why: The subject is the noun or pronoun which performs an action in the Subject and Verb pattern lesson.

mcqs.q: In the S+V pattern, what is a verb?
options: The word that shows an action
mcqs.why: The verb is the word that shows an action, as defined in the S+V pattern section on pages 30-31.

mcqs.q: In 'Jawad plays', what is the verb?
mcqs.why: Plays is the verb showing the action, while Jawad is the subject who performs the action.

mcqs.q: In 'Ammara cooks', what is the subject?
mcqs.why: Ammara is the subject performing the action, and cooks is the verb in this S+V example.

mcqs.q: In 'He writes', what is the subject?
mcqs.why: He is the subject pronoun performing the action, and writes is the verb in example 3.

mcqs.q: In 'She walks', what is the verb?
mcqs.why: Walks is the verb showing the action that the subject She performs in example 4 of S+V.

mcqs.q: How many S+V examples are given in this lesson?
mcqs.why: Four examples are given: Jawad plays, Ammara cooks, He writes and She walks in the S+V section.

mcqs.q: S+V stands for what pattern?
mcqs.why: S+V stands for Subject and Verb, the two parts named in the pattern heading on pages 30-31.

mcqs.q: Which example uses a pronoun as subject?
mcqs.why: He writes uses the pronoun He as subject, and She walks also uses a pronoun as subject.

mcqs.q: Who cooks in the S+V examples?
mcqs.why: Ammara cooks is example 2, where Ammara is the subject and cooks is the verb showing action.

lessons.title: Activity — Write five sentences having subject and verb (p. 31)
lessons.notes_html: Model sentences: 1. Ahmed reads. 2. Sara sings. 3. The bird flies. 4. Ali runs. 5. Mother cooks.

mcqs.q: What are pupils asked to write in this activity on page 31?
options: Five sentences having subject and verb
mcqs.why: The activity asks pupils to write five sentences having subject and verb, with model sentences provided.

mcqs.q: What is model sentence 1 in this activity?
mcqs.why: Model sentence 1 is 'Ahmed reads' where Ahmed is the subject and reads is the verb.

mcqs.q: What is model sentence 2?
mcqs.why: Model sentence 2 is 'Sara sings' with Sara as subject and sings as the verb in the activity.

mcqs.q: What flies in the model sentences?
mcqs.why: Model sentence 3 is 'The bird flies' where the bird is the subject performing the flying action.

mcqs.q: What is model sentence 4?
mcqs.why: Model sentence 4 is 'Ali runs' listed after the bird sentence in the five model sentences.

mcqs.q: What is model sentence 5?
mcqs.why: Model sentence 5 is 'Mother cooks' as the last of the five subject and verb model sentences.

mcqs.q: In 'Ahmed reads', what is the verb?
mcqs.why: Reads is the verb showing the action Ahmed performs, making Ahmed the subject in this model.

mcqs.q: How many model sentences are given in this activity?
mcqs.why: Five model sentences are given, numbered 1 to 5, each having a subject and a verb only.

mcqs.q: Which model sentence has an animal as subject?
mcqs.why: The bird flies has an animal, a bird, as the subject performing the action of flying.

mcqs.q: These model sentences follow which pattern?
mcqs.why: These sentences follow the SV pattern with only subject and verb and no object in each sentence.

lessons.title: S + V + O (Subject, Verb and Object) pattern (p. 31-32)
lessons.notes_html: Object: The noun or pronoun that receives the action is called object. Example: He (Subject) paints (Verb) posters (Object). Who or what performs the action of the verb, is the subject. The verb is the word that expresses what that action is. Whoever or whatever receives that action, is the object.

mcqs.q: In the S+V+O pattern, what is the object?
options: The noun or pronoun that receives the action
mcqs.why: The object is the noun or pronoun that receives the action in the Subject Verb Object pattern lesson.

mcqs.q: In 'He paints posters', what is the object?
mcqs.why: Posters is the object because it receives the action of painting done by the subject He.

mcqs.q: In 'He paints posters', what is the subject?
mcqs.why: He is the subject because he performs the action of the verb paints in the example sentence.

mcqs.q: In 'He paints posters', what is the verb?
mcqs.why: Paints is the verb because it expresses what the action is that the subject performs.

mcqs.q: Who or what performs the action is called what?
mcqs.why: Who or what performs the action of the verb is the subject, as explained in the SVO lesson.

mcqs.q: Whoever or whatever receives the action is called what?
mcqs.why: Whoever or whatever receives that action is the object, completing the SVO pattern explanation.

mcqs.q: The verb is the word that expresses what?
mcqs.why: The verb is the word that expresses what that action is, as stated in the SVO pattern notes.

mcqs.q: S+V+O stands for what?
mcqs.why: S+V+O stands for Subject, Verb and Object, the three parts taught on pages 31-32 of the chapter.

mcqs.q: How many parts are in an SVO sentence?
mcqs.why: An SVO sentence has three parts: a subject, a verb and an object that receives the action.

mcqs.q: Painting posters: posters receive which action?
mcqs.why: Posters receive the painting action expressed by the verb paints done by the subject He.

lessons.title: Activity A — Write five sentences having (SVO) subject, (p. 32)
lessons.notes_html: verb and object Model sentences: 1. Ahmed reads a book. 2. Sara eats an apple. 3. Ali kicks the ball. 4. Mother cooks food. 5. The teacher writes a lesson.

mcqs.q: What are pupils asked to write in Activity A on page 32?
options: Five sentences having subject, verb and object
mcqs.why: Activity A asks for five sentences having subject, verb and object, with SVO model sentences provided.

mcqs.q: What is SVO model sentence 1?
mcqs.why: Model sentence 1 is 'Ahmed reads a book' where Ahmed is subject, reads verb and book object.

mcqs.q: In 'Sara eats an apple', what is the object?
mcqs.why: An apple is the object because it receives the eating action performed by the subject Sara.

mcqs.q: In 'Ali kicks the ball', what is the verb?
mcqs.why: Kicks is the verb showing the action Ali performs on the object, the ball, in model sentence 3.

mcqs.q: What does Mother cook in the model sentences?
mcqs.why: Model sentence 4 is 'Mother cooks food' where food is the object receiving the cooking action.

mcqs.q: Who writes a lesson in the model sentences?
mcqs.why: Model sentence 5 is 'The teacher writes a lesson' with teacher as subject and lesson as object.

mcqs.q: In 'Ahmed reads a book', what is the subject?
mcqs.why: Ahmed is the subject who performs the reading action on the object, a book, in sentence 1.

mcqs.q: How many SVO model sentences are given?
mcqs.why: Five SVO model sentences are given numbered 1 to 5 in Activity A on page 32 of the chapter.

mcqs.q: Which model sentence is about eating?
mcqs.why: Sara eats an apple is the eating sentence, with eats as verb and apple as the object eaten.

mcqs.q: Which model sentence is about kicking?
mcqs.why: Ali kicks the ball is the kicking sentence, where Ali is subject, kicks verb and ball object.

mcqs.why: My father likes meat is the sentence where My father is listed as the subject in the table.

lessons.title: Capitalization (p. 34)
lessons.notes_html: Capitalization is the use of capital letters in writing. It involves the practice of starting sentences with capital letters and capitalizing proper nouns and using capital letters for the pronoun 'I'. Examples: Quetta, Eid, Independence day, Next-Cola, Samsung, Mount Everest, Halloween.

mcqs.q: What is capitalization?
options: Use of capital letters in writing
mcqs.why: Capitalization is the use of capital letters in writing, as defined at the start of the lesson on page 34.

mcqs.q: Capitalization involves starting what with capital letters?
mcqs.why: It involves starting sentences with capital letters and capitalizing proper nouns and the pronoun I.

mcqs.q: Besides sentences, what else is capitalized?
mcqs.why: Proper nouns are capitalized as part of capitalization practice described in the lesson on page 34.

mcqs.q: For which pronoun are capital letters used?
mcqs.why: Capital letters are used for the pronoun I, as stated in the capitalization definition in the notes.

mcqs.q: Which example in the list is a city name?
mcqs.why: Quetta is given among the capitalization examples and it is a geographical / city proper name.

mcqs.q: Which examples are holidays in the list?
mcqs.why: Eid and Halloween (with Independence day) are holiday examples in the capitalization examples list.

mcqs.q: Which example is a product / brand name?
mcqs.why: Next-Cola and Samsung are product names given as examples that need capital letters in writing.

mcqs.q: Which example is a geographical name of a mountain?
mcqs.why: Mount Everest is the geographical name example, a mountain name written with capital letters.

mcqs.q: Independence day is an example of what kind of name?
mcqs.why: Independence day is listed with Eid and Halloween as a special day that is capitalized in the examples.

mcqs.q: How many examples are listed for capitalization?
mcqs.why: Seven examples are listed: Quetta, Eid, Independence day, Next-Cola, Samsung, Mount Everest and Halloween.

options: Bolan River, Ziarat Residency and Chaghi Desert
mcqs.why: Bolan River, Ziarat Residency and Chaghi Desert are geographical / place names needing capitals on both words.

lessons.title: Capital letter for pronoun 'I' and for initials (p. 35)
lessons.notes_html: We also use capital letters for pronoun 'I' and also for initials in names of people. Examples: 1. My favorite color is blue, and I like to draw pictures with blue crayons. 2. I believe I am a responsible student. 3. M.A. Rauf is an author. 4. Allama Iqbal wrote many poems.

mcqs.q: Besides proper nouns, capital letters are used for what in this lesson?
options: Pronoun 'I' and initials in names of people
mcqs.why: This lesson says we also use capital letters for pronoun I and for initials in names of people.

mcqs.q: What is the example sentence about favourite colour?
options: I believe I am a responsible student
My favorite color is blue, and I like to draw pictures with blue crayons
mcqs.why: Example 1 is about favourite color blue and drawing with blue crayons, showing capital I in use.

mcqs.q: What does the speaker believe in example 2?
mcqs.why: Example 2 says 'I believe I am a responsible student' with capital I used twice in the sentence.

mcqs.q: Who is described as an author with initials?
mcqs.why: M.A. Rauf is an author is example 3, showing initials M.A. written with capital letters and dots.

mcqs.q: What did Allama Iqbal do in example 4?
mcqs.why: Example 4 says Allama Iqbal wrote many poems, given alongside the initials and pronoun I examples.

mcqs.q: How many examples are given in this lesson?
mcqs.why: Four examples are numbered 1 to 4 covering pronoun I sentences, M.A. Rauf and Allama Iqbal.

mcqs.q: In 'I believe I can do better', why is I capital? (from outcomes)
options: The word I always takes a capital letter
mcqs.why: The word I is always written with a capital letter wherever it appears in a sentence, as taught here.

mcqs.q: Initials in names are written with what?
mcqs.why: Initials in names of people use capital letters, as in M.A. Rauf where M and A are capitals.

mcqs.q: Which sentence shows I at the start and in the middle?
options: I believe I am a responsible student
mcqs.why: I believe I am a responsible student shows capital I both starting the sentence and in its middle.

mcqs.q: Blue crayons are used to do what in example 1?
mcqs.why: Example 1 says I like to draw pictures with blue crayons, linking favourite colour blue to drawing.

Ahmed is the director of the company. 4. A.S. Edhi established the world's largest ambulance service. 5. Quaid-e-Azam Muhammad Ali Jinnah is the founder of Pakistan.

options: To the zoo and saw a lion roaring

options: Ice cream, especially choosing favourite flavor

mcqs.why: Sentence 3 says Ahmed is the director of the company, a straightforward capitalized sentence in the activity.

mcqs.why: Sentence 4 says A.S. Edhi established the world's largest ambulance service, showing initials A.S. in capitals.

mcqs.q: Who is the founder of Pakistan in sentence 5?
mcqs.why: Sentence 5 says Quaid-e-Azam Muhammad Ali Jinnah is the founder of Pakistan in the activity.

mcqs.q: How many sentences are given to capitalize?
mcqs.why: Five sentences are numbered 1 to 5 in the capitalize-the-sentences activity on page 35.

mcqs.why: A lion roaring loudly was seen at the zoo in sentence 1 of the capitalization activity.

mcqs.why: A.S. Edhi carries the initials A.S., parallel to M.A. Rauf as an initials example with capitals.

mcqs.why: Sentences 1 and 2 feature I repeatedly about the zoo visit and enjoying ice cream respectively.

lessons.title: Writing — Capital Letters (p. 35)
lessons.notes_html: 1. Capital letters are used at the beginning of sentences. 2. They are also used for the first letter of proper nouns. Examples: 1. We are going to school. 2. I visited Minar-e-Pakistan at Lahore.

mcqs.q: Where are capital letters used, according to Writing on page 35?
mcqs.why: Writing point 1 says capital letters are used at the beginning of sentences as a basic rule.

mcqs.q: Capital letters are also used for what, in point 2?
mcqs.why: Point 2 says they are also used for the first letter of proper nouns in the Writing section.

mcqs.q: What is example 1 in the Writing section?
mcqs.why: Example 1 is 'We are going to school' showing W capital at the beginning of the sentence.

mcqs.q: What is example 2 in the Writing section?
mcqs.why: Example 2 is 'I visited Minar-e-Pakistan at Lahore' showing capitals for proper nouns and pronoun I.

mcqs.q: Which place was visited in example 2?
mcqs.why: Minar-e-Pakistan at Lahore was visited, with capitals on Minar-e-Pakistan and Lahore as proper nouns.

mcqs.q: How many rules are stated in the Writing section?
mcqs.why: Two rules are stated: capitals at sentence beginnings and for first letter of proper nouns.

mcqs.q: How many examples are given in the Writing section?
mcqs.why: Two examples are given numbered 1 and 2 to illustrate the two capitalization rules stated.

mcqs.q: 'We are going to school' illustrates which rule?
mcqs.why: It illustrates the beginning of sentence rule because We starts the sentence with a capital W.

mcqs.q: 'I visited Minar-e-Pakistan' illustrates which use?
options: Proper nouns and pronoun I capitals
mcqs.why: It shows both pronoun I capital and proper noun capitals for Minar-e-Pakistan and Lahore together.

mcqs.q: Writing section is on which page?
mcqs.why: The Writing — Capital Letters section is headed as page 35 in the notes for Chapter 1.

lessons.title: Full Stop (.) and Question Mark (?) (p. 36)
lessons.notes_html: Full stop is used at the end of sentences that are statements or commands. Examples: 1. I like to read books. 2. Sit down, please. Question mark is used at the end of a direct question. Examples: 1. What is your name? 2. What is your favourite colour?

mcqs.q: When is a full stop used?
options: At the end of sentences that are statements or commands
mcqs.why: A full stop is used at the end of sentences that are statements or commands, as defined on page 36.

mcqs.q: When is a question mark used?
options: At the end of a direct question
mcqs.why: A question mark is used at the end of a direct question, as defined in the punctuation lesson.

mcqs.q: Which is a full stop example?
mcqs.why: I like to read books ends with a full stop because it is a statement, given as example 1.

mcqs.q: Which is a full stop command example?
mcqs.why: Sit down, please ends with a full stop because commands take full stops, as example 2 shows.

mcqs.q: Which is a question mark example?
mcqs.why: What is your name ends with a question mark because it is a direct question asked to someone.

mcqs.q: What is the second question example about?
mcqs.why: The second question example asks 'What is your favourite colour?' ending with a question mark.

mcqs.q: How many full stop examples are given?
mcqs.why: Two full stop examples are given: I like to read books and Sit down, please, on page 36.

mcqs.q: How many question mark examples are given?
mcqs.why: Two question mark examples are given: What is your name and What is your favourite colour.

mcqs.q: A statement sentence should end with what?
mcqs.why: A statement should end with a full stop, distinguishing it from a direct question ending differently.

mcqs.q: A direct question should end with what?
mcqs.why: A direct question should end with a question mark, as both question examples in the lesson show.

mcqs.why: Six sentences are numbered 1 to 6 in the re-write with correct punctuation activity on pages 36-37.

lessons.title: Student Learning Outcomes (p. 38)
lessons.notes_html: use pre-reading strategies to predict some words that might occur in a text by looking at the picture/title; respond to text with reasons and personal opinions; use strategies to learn blend unfamiliar words to read, including sounding out and separating them into syllables; make anagrams from simple one/two syllable words; provide missing letters in simple two/three syllable letters; identify and recognize the rules for the use of 'a', 'an' and 'the'; use of a, an with countable and uncountable nouns; listen and understand longer conversations from different contexts, short lectures and talks, radio and TV broadcasts, stories, and descriptions of events and will be able to identify main ideas; use of contractions with verbs (e.g., I'm, I've, she's, it's); spell and write familiar and unfamiliar words accurately.

mcqs.q: What spelling outcome is listed at the end?

lessons.title: Lesson text — The Woodpecker (p. 39)
lessons.notes_html: There are many beautiful birds in the world and one of them is 'woodpecker'. The woodpecker is an interesting bird. It is found in different colours and sizes. It has a strong, pointed beak that acts as a hammer to remove bark (tough material that covers the outside of a tree) from trees and find insects to eat. It has a long tongue, two to four inches long, that is sticky on the tip for catching insects. Most birds have one toe pointing back and three pointing forward on each foot. Woodpeckers are a little bit different. They have two sharp claws pointing back and two sharp claws pointing forward on each foot to help them hold on to the sides of trees. The life span of a woodpecker is 4-11 years (National Wildlife Federation). Their favourite foods are insects, fruit and nuts. These interesting birds live in forests and wooded areas with lots of trees. Woodpeckers can be found all over the world, except Australia. Picture labels: beak, front claws, back claws.

lessons.title: Syllable (p. 41)
lessons.notes_html: A syllable is a word that is pronounced as a single sound. One Syllable Word: it is a unit of pronunciation having one vowel or one single sound. For example: cat, bat, hat, fish, walk, etc. Two Syllable Word: the words having two syllables are called two syllable words. For example: apple /ap/ /ple/, orange /or/ /ange/, walking /walk/ /ing/, etc. Three Syllable Word: the words having three syllables are called three syllable words. For example: important /im/ /por/ /tant/, excellent /ex/ /cel/ /lent/, etc.

lessons.title: Oral Communication Skills — Lecture: Recycling (p. 42-43)
lessons.notes_html: Teacher enters the classroom with a smiling face. Teacher: Good morning, class! Today, we're going to learn about something important - recycling! Can anyone tell me what this symbol means? Yes, Sarah? Sarah: It means recycling. Teacher: That's right! Recycling is when we give our old things a new life. When we recycle, we help to save our planet by reducing waste and saving natural resources. Look around you, class! We can recycle paper, plastic, glass, and metal! Recycling is easy! All we have to do is put our recyclables in the right bin. (Pointing to bins) Let me show you: The yellow bin is for putting plastic. The green bin is for green plants and leaves. The red bin is for general rubbish or waste. When we use the correct bins, we keep our environment clean and happy. Recycling is like giving our planet a big hug! lessons.title: Grammar — Definite and Indefinite Articles (p. 44-46)
lessons.notes_html:
Indefinite Articles (a, an): 'A' or 'An' is called indefinite articles because it

does not point out any particular person or a thing. 'a': We use 'a' before words that start with a consonant sound. Examples: a pen, a hat, a doll, a ball, a flower. 'an': There are five vowels in English alphabet: a, e, i, o, u. 'an' is used before the word beginning with a vowel sound. Examples: an ant, an egg, an inkpot, an orange, an umbrella. Read the following sentences and observe how 'a' or 'an' is used correctly: 1. I have a cow. (correct sentence) / I have a cows. (incorrect sentence) 2. It is an orange. (correct sentence) / It is a orange. (incorrect sentence). Definite Article (The): Rule for 'the': We use 'the' when talking about something specific or previously mentioned. Examples: 1. The dog in the yard is barking loudly. 2. Please pass me the book on the table. 3. He went to the store to buy some milk. 4. The girl with the red hat is my sister. 5. We visited the Lahore zoo last summer and had a great time.

lessons.title: Use of a, an with Countable and Uncountable Nouns (p. 46)
lessons.notes_html: We use 'a' and 'an' with countable nouns, but we do not use them with uncountable nouns. 1. 'a' and 'an' with Countable Nouns: a ball, a cat, a tree, a book; an apple, an elephant, an orange, an umbrella. 2. No 'a' or 'an' with Uncountable Nouns: uncountable nouns do not take 'a' or 'an' because they cannot be counted. Incorrect - Correct: a water - water; an advice - advice; a rice - rice. Examples in sentences: 1. I ate an orange. 2. He has a new pencil. 3. She drank water. (no article) 4. We need sugar. (not a sugar)

lessons.title: Punctuation — Contractions (p. 47)
lessons.notes_html: Contractions are short forms, commonly used in English to combine pronouns and verbs. Examples: 1. I'm (I am): I'm going to the store. 2. I've (I have): I've finished my homework. 3. She's (She is or She has): She's coming to the party. She's already eaten. 4. It's (It is or It has): It's raining outside. It's been a long day. 5. He's (He is or He has): He's speaking English. He's offered prayers. 6. They're (They are): They're playing football. 7. We're (We are): We're good students. 8. You're (You are): You're a good player of hockey.

Imagine, we're having a chat. You have a great idea to share. What would you do? Gohar: I guess, I had raise my hand and wait for the teacher to call on me. Then, I had share my idea. Fahad: Perfect! lessons.title: Grammar — Subjective, Objective and Possessive Pronouns (p. 57-58)
lessons.notes_html:
Subjective Pronouns: Subjective pronouns are used as the subject of a sentence. They perform the action of the verb or specify who or what is doing the action. e.g. I, you, he, she, it, we, they. Examples: 1. I am going

to the store. 2. You are my best friend. 3. He likes to play soccer. 4. She is reading a book. 5. We are going to the beach. Objective Pronouns: Objective pronouns are used as objects of verbs or prepositions. They receive the action of the verb or show the relationship between the verb and other words in the sentence, e.g. me, you, him, her, it, us, them. Examples: 1. She gave him a book. 2. Please pass the salt to me. 3. They invited us to the party. 4. I saw them at the store. 5. He loves his parents. (Note: the book lists 'his' under objective pronouns in example 5 - 'his' is a possessive word, not an objective pronoun, flagged; the same point was flagged in Grade 2.) Possessive Pronouns: Possessive pronouns indicate ownership or possession. They show that something belongs to someone or something else, e.g. mine, yours, his, hers, its, ours, theirs. Examples: 1. The car is mine. 2. Is this pen yours or mine? 3. The cat licked its paws. 4. The house is theirs. 5. The book is hers.

lessons.title: Student Learning Outcomes (p. 64)
lessons.notes_html:
use pre-reading strategies to

predict some words that might occur in a text by looking at the picture/title; answer questions with some reference to single points in a text using pre and while reading strategies; ask questions for clarity and respond to questions from others; answer questions in multiple choice; recognize questions as interrogative sentences that begin with 'wh' questions; use interrogative pronouns to make question sentences; identify and classify the grammatical gender of naming words from immediate environment (masculine/feminine); recognize and use grade-level words that show feelings and emotions (e.g., bored, scared, shy, afraid, upset); use simple present verbs to show habitual actions; make questions by using wh-questions; use strategies for segmenting unfamiliar words to spell, e.g., breaking into individual sounds, separating into syllables.

lessons.title: Lesson text — My Beautiful Country Pakistan (p. 65-67)
lessons.notes_html:
My beautiful country, Pakistan, is very special to me. It is in South Asia.

Pakistan is a beautiful country. Let's learn about the different provinces, people, languages, games, culture, and amazing places to visit. Provinces of Pakistan: Pakistan has four provinces: Punjab, Sindh, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan. Punjab: Punjab is known for its green fields where farmers grow important crops like wheat and rice. You can see large farms all over the land. The people of Punjab love delicious food and enjoy playing cricket, kabbadi and hockey. Punjab is home to big cities like Lahore, Faisalabad, Multan, and Rawalpindi. Lahore is full of history and has beautiful buildings like the famous Badshahi Mosque and Shahi Qilla. Sindh: Sindh is full of rich culture and history. You can visit the ancient city of Mohenjo-Daro, which is a very old city! The people of Sindh love to wear their traditional ajrak and Sindhi topi. Big cities like Karachi and Hyderabad are situated in Sindh. You can visit the Mazar-e-Quaid in Karachi where Quaid-e-Azam is buried. Khyber Pakhtunkhwa: Khyber Pakhtunkhwa has tall, snowy mountains and beautiful green valleys. You can see children in traditional Peshawari dress, smiling and playing. The famous Khyber Pass is also found here. Big cities here include Peshawar, Swat, and Dera Ismail Khan. The people are known for being very brave and friendly. Balochistan: Balochistan is the largest province of Pakistan. It has large deserts, high mountains, and beautiful places like the Ziarat Residency and the seaside city of Gwadar. The main cities of Balochistan are Quetta, Gwadar, and Khuzdar. The people of this province are kind, strong and friendly. Languages: Urdu is the national language of Pakistan, but other languages like Punjabi, Sindhi, Pashto, Balochi, Brahvi etc., are also spoken. Games: Pakistan is a country where people love to play different games. People enjoy playing cricket, football, hockey, and badminton. Hockey is the national game of Pakistan. Many people also like traditional games such as kabaddi and gullidanda. Handicrafts:

Pakistan is famous for its beautiful handicrafts. You can find delicate pottery in Multan, colorful embroidery in Karachi, beautiful woodwork in Swat, Balochi embroidered dresses, caps and shawls in Balochistan, and soft carpets in Peshawar. Festivals: We celebrate different cultural festivals like Eid, Independence day, Christmas and Holi. On these days people wear beautiful dresses and enjoy yummy food. Places to Visit: In Pakistan, there are many amazing places to visit! You can explore the ancient ruins of Mohenjo-Daro in Sindh, go hiking in the beautiful valleys of Swat in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, visit the stunning beaches of Gwadar in Balochistan, or see the historic Badshahi Mosque in Lahore, Punjab.

lessons.title: Oral Communication Skills — Dialogue between (p. 69-70)
lessons.notes_html: father and daughter (Saima and her father Mr. Jalal) Mr. Jalal: Hey, Saima, do you know that the Earth is mostly covered by water? Saima: Really, Dad? But how do we know that if we can't see it all? Mr. Jalal: That's a great question, Saima. Scientists use satellites and other technology to study the Earth from space. They can measure the amount of water covering the Earth's surface and estimate the total volume of water on our planet. Saima: Wow! that's so interesting. But why is water so important for life on Earth? Mr. Jalal: Another excellent question, Saima. Water is essential for life because it helps plants grow, provides habitats for animals, and is necessary for humans to drink and stay healthy. Without water, life as we know it would not be possible. Saima: I see. So, water is like the lifeblood of our planet. Mr. Jalal: Exactly! Saima. It's amazing how something so simple can be so vital for life. Remember, asking questions and seeking knowledge is a great way to learn more about the world around us. Saima: Thanks, Dad. I love learning new things with you. Mr. Jalal: You are welcome! (Speaking activity - practise the dialogue in pairs.)

lessons.title: Tenses — Simple Present Tense (p. 73-74)
lessons.notes_html:
The Simple Present Tense is used to talk about actions or events that happen regularly, or as a habit. Formation: He, she, it + first form of the verb with s/es; I, you, we, they + first form of the verb without s/es. Positive Sentences: 1. She reads a book every night before going to bed. 2. They go for jogging in the park every morning. 3. He wakes up early every day. 4. We eat dinner together as a family every evening. 5. The birds sing in the trees every morning. Negative Sentences: Subject + do/does not + first form of the verb. 1. She does not read a book every night before going to bed. 2. They do not go for jogging in the park every morning. 3. He does not wake up early every day. Interrogative Sentences: Do/Does + subject + first form of the verb + ? 1. Does she

read a book every night before going to bed? 2. Do they go for jogging in the park every morning? 3. Does he wake up early every day?

lessons.title: Lesson text — The Importance of Cleanliness (p. 78-80)
lessons.notes_html:
Cleanliness is very important for keeping ourselves healthy and our world beautiful. When we talk about cleanliness, we mean making sure everything around us is neat, tidy, and free from dirt and germs. Let's learn why cleanliness is so important and how we can keep our surroundings clean. Cleanliness Matters: Firstly, cleanliness helps us stay healthy. When we keep our body clean by washing our hands, taking bath, and brushing our teeth, we can prevent germs from making us sick.

Cleanliness also keeps our homes and schools safe and comfortable places to be. Imagine how bad it would be if there were trash and dirt everywhere. Keeping Our Surroundings Clean: There are many simple things we can do to keep our surroundings clean. One important thing is to always throw our trash in the proper bins. We can have separate bins for different kinds of waste, like paper, plastic, and food scraps, and make sure to put our trash in the right one. Another way to keep our surroundings clean is to pick up litter when we see it. If we see trash on the ground, we can pick it up and throw it away in trash bin. Cleaning Up After Ourselves: It is also important to clean up wherever we go. If we make a mess while eating, we can use napkins to wipe up spills and crumbs. After playing with toys or games, we can put them back where they belong instead of leaving them scattered around. By cleaning up, we show respect for our belongings and the people around us. Taking Care of Nature: We should also take care of nature by not littering and by helping to keep parks, playgrounds, and other outdoor spaces clean. When we visit these places, we can make sure to pick up any trash we see and dispose it off properly. We can also help by planting trees and flowers, which make our environment cleaner and more beautiful. We can say that cleanliness is very important for keeping ourselves healthy and our world clean. By practicing good hygiene, keeping our surroundings clean, and taking care of nature, we can all do our part to make the world a better place. So let's remember to always stay clean and tidy, both for ourselves and for our planet.

lessons.title: Sounds and Spellings — Sounds with Different Spellings for Five Major Vowels (p. 81-82)
lessons.notes_html:
A (as in 'cat'): Sound: /ae/ (short 'a' sound). Spellings: (1) 'a' as in 'cat', (2) 'e' as in 'ate', (3) 'ai' as in 'rain', (4) 'ay' as in 'say'. Examples: cat, bat, sat, ate, gate, rain, say. E (as in 'bed'): Sound: /e/ (short 'e' sound). Spellings: (1) 'e' as in 'bed', (2) 'ea' as in 'head', (3) 'ai' as in 'said', (4) 'e-e' as in 'theme'. Examples: bed, red, fed, head, bread, said, theme. I (as in 'sit'): Sound: /I/ (short 'I' sound). Spellings: (1) 'i' as in 'sit', (2) 'y' as in 'my', (3) 'ie' as in 'pie', (4) 'igh' as in 'high'. Examples: sit, bit, fit, my, by, pie, high. O (as in 'hot'): Sound: /a/ (short 'o' sound). Spellings: (1) 'o'

as in 'hot', (2) 'a' as in 'not', (3) 'au' as in 'caught', (4) 'aw' as in 'saw'. Examples: hot, pot, dot, not, caught, saw. U (as in 'cut'): Sound: /u/ (short 'u' sound). Spellings: (1) 'u' as in 'cut', (2) 'o' as in 'love', (3) 'oo' as in 'book', (4) 'ou' as in 'should'. Examples: cut, hut, nut, love, dove, book, should.

lessons.title: Grammar — Singular/Plural with Regular and Irregular Nouns (p. 85)
lessons.notes_html: Regular Nouns: Regular nouns are those that form their plural by adding '-s' or '-es' to the singular form. In other words, they follow predictable patterns when pluralizing. Examples: dog - dogs; house - houses; book - books; car - cars. Irregular Nouns: Irregular nouns are those that do not follow the typical patterns for forming plurals. Instead, they have unique or irregular plural forms that often differ significantly from their singular counterparts. Examples: child - children; man - men; woman - women; tooth - teeth.

lessons.title: Tenses — Present Continuous Tense (p. 87-88)
lessons.notes_html:
Present Continuous Tense: Simple Present Continuous Tense is used to describe actions that are happening at the moment of speaking. Examples: 1. I am speaking English right now. 2. We are reading. 3. They are listening to us. 4. She is watching cartoons. Formation: The Simple Present Continuous Tense is formed using the present tense of the verb 'to be' (am, is, are) followed by the first form of the main verb with the -ing ending. Affirmative: Subject + am/is/are + first form of verb + ing.

Examples: 1. You are writing. 2. They are playing. Negative: Subject + am/is/are + not + verb + ing. Examples: 1. I am not laughing. 2. She is not studying. Interrogative/Question: Am/Is/Are + subject + verb + ing? Examples: 1. Are you laughing? 2. Is she sleeping?

lessons.title: Lesson text — Something Special on Birthday (p. 92-93)
lessons.notes_html:
Sana was getting ready for her birthday, and there was so much to do. She and her mom had a big list of things to buy for her party. Birthday Shopping List: biscuits, ice cream, party hats, balloons, apples, bananas, candles, milk, juice, pastries, cake, drinks. They were determined to make it the best celebration ever. With their list in hand, Sana and her mother headed to the market. They walked past colourful stalls, picking up everything they needed: biscuits, ice-cream, balloons, chocolates, and lots of yummy treats. They also got fruits, milk, bread, and all the things for a fun party. But while they were shopping, Sana remembered something special her grandma used to do on her birthdays. She would

share treats with children who didn't have much. Sana thought that was a wonderful idea. When they got back home, Sana showed her grandma all the party stuff they bought. She also shared her idea about sharing treats with others. Her grandma smiled and said it was a lovely idea. Sana decided to use her pocket money to buy lots of toffees. She went to the store and got bags full of them. Then, she gave them to children who didn't have many sweets. Seeing their happy faces made her own birthday even more special. Sana knew that even a small act of kindness could make a big difference, and that made her birthday the best one.

lessons.title: Oral Communication Skills — Expressing meanings (p. 97-99)
lessons.notes_html:
through talk and non-verbal communication: a surprise birthday party Characters: Ali (Birthday boy), Ayesha (Ali's best friend), Bilal (Ali's classmate), Sara (Ali's cousin), Mama (Ali's mother). Scene: Ali's house is decorated with balloons and streamers. His friends are gathered for his birthday party. Mama: (Claps hands) Kids. Are you all ready for the surprise? Ali will be here any moment. Jamal, Bilal, Sara: (Excitedly whispering) Yes, we are ready. (Ali enters the room) All: (Loudly) Surprise! Happy Birthday, Ali. Ali: (Eyes wide open, smiling brightly) Wow! Is this all for me? Thank you. Jamal: (Handing a gift) Here, this is a small

present for you. Ali: (Happily takes the gift) Thank you. Bilal: (Excitedly) Ali, quickly blow the candles and make a wish. Sara: (Clapping hands) Yes, we are all waiting. (Ali closes his eyes, makes a wish, and blows out the candles. Everyone claps) Mama: (Smiling) Now, let's cut the cake. Ali: (Cutting the cake) The first piece is for Mama. Mama: (Hugs Ali) You are such a sweet boy. Jamal: (Notices Bilal looking sad) Bilal, are you okay? Why are you so quiet? Bilal: (Softly) Nothing. I just wish I could celebrate my birthday like this too... But we don't have big parties at home. Ali: (Pats Bilal's shoulder) Oh Bilal, don't worry. When your birthday comes, we will have a surprise party for you too. Sara: (Excitedly) Yes. We will decorate your house and make it special. Bilal: (Smiles) Really? That would be amazing. Thank you, friends. (All friends laugh and enjoy cake together). (Note: the character list names Ayesha as Ali's best friend, but the dialogue lines are given to Jamal, who is not in the character list - flagged, reproduced as printed. Activity, page 99: Perform a role play about your birthday experiences in front of the class.)

lessons.title: Grammar — Adjective (Describing Words) (p. 100)
lessons.notes_html:
Describing words are called adjectives. Adjectives are words that describe or modify nouns. They tell us more about the characteristics or qualities of a noun and pronoun. Examples: 1. The red apple fell from the tree. 2. She wore a soft blanket on a chilly night. 3. The big elephant

walked slowly.

lessons.title: Degrees of Adjectives: Comparative and Superlative (p. 101)
lessons.notes_html:
Comparative Adjectives: Comparative adjectives are used to compare two things or people. Examples: 1. The cat is faster than the dog. 2. She is taller than her sister. 3. This book is more interesting than that one. Superlative Adjectives: Superlative adjectives are used to compare three or more things or people, showing which one has the highest degree of a quality. Examples: 1. The cheetah is the fastest land animal. 2. She is the tallest girl in her class. 3. This is the most delicious cake I have ever tasted. Difference between Comparative and Superlative Adjectives: Comparative Example: The cat is faster than the dog. (Comparing two things - cat and dog). Superlative Example: The cheetah is the fastest

land animal. (Comparing the cheetah to all other land animals).

mcqs.why: Superlative adjectives compare three or more things, showing the highest degree of quality.

lessons.title: Tenses — Present Perfect Tense (p. 102-103)
lessons.notes_html:
Present Perfect Tense: The present perfect tense shows that an action or event happened at some point in the past, but its effect is still in present. Positive Sentence: Subject + have/has + Third form of the verb. Examples: 1. I have eaten breakfast. 2. She has finished her homework. 3. They have played in the park. 4. He has read a book. Negative Sentence: Subject + have/has + not + third form of the verb. Examples: 1. I have not watched that movie. 2. She has not visited the museum. 3. They have not finished their lunch. 4. He has not cleaned his room.

Interrogative Sentence: (Have/Has) + subject + third form of the verb + ? Examples: 1. Have I finished my work? 2. Has she eaten her lunch? 3. Have they completed their assignment? 4. Has he read the story?

mcqs.q: The present perfect tense shows an action happened in the past but its effect is still where?
mcqs.why: It shows an action happened in the past, but its effect is still in the present.

mcqs.why: The positive structure is Subject plus have or has plus the third form of the verb.

mcqs.q: Which sentence is a negative present perfect sentence?
options: She has not visited the museum.
They have played in the park.
mcqs.why: She has not visited uses has plus not plus the third form, making it negative present perfect.

mcqs.q: How does an interrogative present perfect sentence begin?
mcqs.why: Interrogative sentences begin with Have or Has, then subject and third form, plus a question mark.

mcqs.q: 'He has read a book' uses has because the subject is what?
mcqs.why: He takes has in present perfect, as shown in the example He has read a book.

mcqs.q: Which is the correct negative form structure?
mcqs.why: The negative structure is Subject plus have or has plus not plus third form of verb.

mcqs.q: 'Have they completed their assignment?' is which type of sentence?
mcqs.why: It begins with Have and ends with a question mark, so it is an interrogative sentence.

mcqs.q: In 'They have not finished their lunch', which word makes it negative?
mcqs.why: Not makes the sentence negative, placed after have in the present perfect structure given.

lessons.title: Story text — The Tale of Honest Hannah (p. 107-108)
lessons.notes_html:
Once upon a time, in small village between green hills and winding rivers, there lived a girl named Hannah. She was known for her bright smile and kind heart. But there was one thing about Hannah that made her special and that was she never told lies. She believed that honesty is the best policy, and she always tried to speak the truth, no matter what. Her friends admired her honesty and often came to her for advice and support. One sunny morning, as she was walking through the village square, she saw a shiny red apple lying on the ground. Curious, she picked it up and looked around to see if anyone had dropped it. But there was no one in sight. She knew that the apple didn't belong to her, so she decided to take it to the village market and ask if anyone had lost it. As she walked through the bustling market stalls, she noticed a little boy crying. 'What's wrong?' she asked gently. 'I lost my favorite apple,' The

boy sniffled. 'I was saving it for a special treat.' Hannah's heart went out to the boy. 'Is this your apple?' she asked, holding out the shiny red fruit. The boy's eyes lit up with joy as he took the apple from Hannah's hand. 'Yes, that's it! Thank you so much!' he exclaimed, and said thank you aloud. She smiled and waved goodbye to the boy before continuing on her way. As she walked, she thought about how good it felt to be honest and help someone in need. She knew that speaking the truth was always the right thing to do, even when it was hard. From that day on, Hannah continued to live her life with honesty and integrity. And though she faced many challenges along the way, she always stayed true to herself and never told a lie. And so, the villagers of the little village came to admire and respect Hannah even more, for she was not only brave and kind but also honest and shining example for all to follow.

lessons.title: Vocabulary — Prefix (p. 111)
lessons.notes_html:
A prefix is added to the beginning of a word to change its meaning or create a new word. Prefixes are commonly used in language to modify the root or base word. Examples: 1. Pre- + love = Preloved: Previously loved or used. (Original word: Love) 'I found a beautiful preloved dress at the store.' 2. Dis- + agreeable = Disagreeable: Not agreeable. (Original word: Agreeable) 'The two colleagues are in disagreeable situation.' 3. Un- + comfortable = Uncomfortable: Causing discomfort or unease; not

comfortable. (Original word: Comfortable) 'These tight shoes are making me uncomfortable.' 4. Care + less = Careless: Not paying attention or showing concern; negligent. (Original word: Care) 'He is a careless driver.' (Note: '-less' in 'careless' is a suffix, not a prefix, although the book lists it under Prefix - flagged.) 5. Pre- + heat = Preheat: To heat something in advance or before using. (original word: heat) 'Before baking the cookies, remember to preheat the oven to 350 degrees F.'

lessons.title: Grammar — Adverb (p. 112)
lessons.notes_html:
Adverb: An adverb is a word that modifies or provides additional information about a verb, adjective, or another adverb in a sentence. Adverb of Manner: An adverb of manner describes how an action is performed or the manner in which something happens. It provides more information about the verb in a sentence. Examples: 1. She sings beautifully. 2. He runs slowly. 3. They danced gracefully. 4. The dog barked loudly. 5. He speaks fluently. Adverb of Time: An adverb of time indicates when an action occurs or the frequency with which it occurs. It specifies the timing or duration of the action. Examples include words like

'yesterday', 'tomorrow', 'now', 'soon', 'often', 'always', and 'daily'. Examples: 1. We will meet tomorrow. 2. She arrived early. 3. They left yesterday. 4. I have to finish this by noon. 5. They usually go for a walk in the evening.

mcqs.q: What is an adverb?
options: A word that modifies a verb, adjective or another adverb
mcqs.why: An adverb modifies or gives more information about a verb, adjective or another adverb.

mcqs.q: An adverb of manner describes what?
mcqs.why: An adverb of manner describes how an action is performed or the manner it happens in.

mcqs.q: In 'She sings beautifully', the adverb of manner is what?
mcqs.why: Beautifully tells how she sings, so it is the adverb of manner in that example sentence.

mcqs.q: In 'He runs slowly', 'slowly' tells us what?
mcqs.why: Slowly describes how he runs, so it is an adverb of manner in the example sentence.

mcqs.q: An adverb of time indicates what?
options: When an action occurs or its frequency
mcqs.why: An adverb of time indicates when an action occurs or how often it occurs in a sentence.

mcqs.q: Which word is an adverb of time in the examples?
mcqs.why: Yesterday is listed among adverbs of time like tomorrow, now, soon, often and always.

mcqs.why: Tomorrow tells when we will meet, so it is an adverb of time in that example.

mcqs.why: Loudly tells how the dog barked, so it is an adverb of manner in the example sentence.

mcqs.why: Gracefully describes how they danced, making it an adverb of manner in the example.

lessons.notes_html: Regular Degrees: slowly - more slowly - most slowly; quickly - more quickly - most quickly; quietly - more quietly - most quietly. Irregular Degrees: well - better - best; badly - worse - worst; much - more - most.

lessons.title: Tenses — Simple Past Tense (p. 114-115)
lessons.notes_html: Simple Past Tense: The simple past tense is used to talk about actions or events that happened at a specific time in the past. Positive Sentence: Subject + second form of the verb + object. Examples: 1. I played with my friends. 2. He cleaned his room. 3. I ate breakfast. 4. She ran in the park. Negative Sentence: Subject + did not + first form of the verb + object. Examples: 1. I did not finish my homework. 2. She did not go to the store. 3. They did not play outside. 4. He did not watch TV. Interrogative Sentence: Did + subject + first form of the verb + object. Examples: 1. Did I complete the puzzle? 2. Did she eat her lunch? 3. Did they play a match? 4. Did he read the story?

mcqs.q: The simple past tense is used to talk about what?

mcqs.why: Simple past talks about actions or events that happened at a specific time in the past.

lessons.title: Lesson text — Boys and Girls Are Equally Important (p. 122-123)
lessons.notes_html:
Once upon a time, in a small house there lived a brother and sister named Sami and Laiba with their family. Sami was full of energy and loved to play with his toy cars and build towering block towers, while Laiba was kind-hearted and enjoyed dressing up her dolls and arranging tea parties. One sunny afternoon, their parents decided to host a special event to teach them about the importance of equality. As the event began, Sami walked proudly with his chest out, saying he was better at everything than Laiba. 'I'm the best at racing cars and building tall towers. Girls can not do that' he exclaimed proudly, while Laiba looked on with a sad expression. Their father noticed Sami's behavior and gently called him over. 'Sami, come sit with me for a moment' he said,

motioning for Laiba to join them as well. As they sat down, their father began to speak. 'Sami, Laiba, I want to talk to you both about something very important,' he started. 'You see, boys and girls are like two sides of the same coin. Each of you is special and unique in your own way, and neither is better than the other.' Sami looked confused, while Laiba nodded in agreement. Their father continued, 'Sami, just because you are a boy does not mean you are better than Laiba. And Laiba, just because you are a girl does not mean you are not as good as Sami. Boys and girls are equal, and it is important to treat each other with kindness, respect, and love.' Sami's eyes widened as he realized the truth of his father's words. 'But Father, I did not mean to make Laiba feel bad,' he said quietly. 'It's okay, Sami,' their father spoke softly. 'We all make mistakes sometimes. What's important is that we learn from them and try to do better next time.' From that day on, Sami and Laiba made a promise to each other and their parents to always treat each other with kindness and respect, knowing that boys and girls are equal and deserving of love and acceptance. And so, as the event came to a close, Sami and Laiba shook hands, grateful for the lesson they had learned about the importance of equality. And as they played together, they knew that they were different, they would always be equal in each other's eyes.

lessons.title: Story, Poetry and Informational Books (p. 125)
lessons.notes_html: 1. Storybooks: A storybook tells us stories about people, animals, fun adventures etc. A story has a beginning, a middle and an end. 2. Poetry Books: A poetry book is a collection of poems, verses and other kinds of poetry. Poems are special kinds of writing that often use rhyming words and a rhythm to make them fun to read. 3. Informational Books: An informational book tells us facts and gives us true information about things in the world. It can be about animals, plants and places etc.

mcqs.q: What does a storybook tell us?
options: Stories about people, animals and fun adventures
mcqs.why: A storybook tells us stories about people, animals, fun adventures and similar story content.

mcqs.q: What three parts does a story have?
options: A title, a picture and a chapter
A beginning, a middle and an end
A noun, a verb and an adjective
mcqs.why: The notes say a story has a beginning, a middle and an end as its three main parts.

mcqs.q: What is a poetry book?
options: A book of true facts only
A collection of poems, verses and other kinds of poetry
mcqs.why: A poetry book is defined as a collection of poems, verses and other kinds of poetry.

mcqs.q: What do poems often use to make them fun to read?
mcqs.why: Poems are special writing that often uses rhyming words and a rhythm to make them fun to read.

mcqs.q: What does an informational book tell us?
options: Facts and true information about things in the world
mcqs.why: An informational book tells us facts and gives us true information about things in the world.

mcqs.q: An informational book can be about which things?
mcqs.why: The notes give animals, plants and places as examples of topics for an informational book.

mcqs.q: Which kind of book is a collection of poems?
mcqs.why: A poetry book is the kind of book that is a collection of poems, verses and other poetry.

mcqs.q: Which kind of book gives true information?
mcqs.why: An informational book gives facts and true information about things in the world around us.

mcqs.q: Poems are described as a special kind of:
mcqs.why: Poems are described as special kinds of writing that often use rhyming words and a rhythm.

mcqs.q: A story about people and fun adventures belongs in a:
mcqs.why: Stories about people, animals and fun adventures are what a storybook tells us, says the lesson.

lessons.title: Organization of Ideas in a Book (p. 125-126)
lessons.notes_html: Chapter: A chapter is a part of a book. It is like a section that is all about one main idea or topic. Main Idea: Each chapter is about one idea. For example, a chapter might be about 'How to clean the classroom'. Pictures: Chapters often have pictures to help us understand the main idea/topic better. Chapter Break: We start a new idea from a new chapter in a book. Paragraph: A paragraph is a smaller part of the writing that lives inside a chapter. A paragraph is about one idea. It keeps ideas together so that they are easy to read and understand. A new paragraph starts on a new line.

mcqs.q: What is a chapter in a book?
options: A single word made of two words
A part of a book, like a section about one main idea or topic
mcqs.why: A chapter is a part of a book, like a section that is all about one main idea or topic.

mcqs.q: What is each chapter about?
options: One idea, called the main idea
mcqs.why: The notes say each chapter is about one idea, for example a chapter about 'How to clean the classroom'.

mcqs.q: What example of a chapter topic is given in the notes?
options: How to race a toy car
How to arrange a tea party
mcqs.why: The example given for a chapter's main idea is a chapter about 'How to clean the classroom'.

mcqs.q: Why do chapters often have pictures?
options: To help us understand the main idea or topic better
mcqs.why: Chapters often have pictures to help us understand the main idea or topic better, say the notes.

mcqs.q: When do we start a new chapter?
options: When we start a new idea in a book
When we use a joining word
mcqs.why: A chapter break means we start a new idea from a new chapter in a book, according to the notes.

mcqs.q: What is a paragraph?
options: A whole book in one section
A smaller part of the writing that lives inside a chapter
mcqs.why: A paragraph is a smaller part of the writing that lives inside a chapter and is about one idea.

mcqs.q: What is a paragraph about?
mcqs.why: The notes say a paragraph is about one idea, just as a chapter is about one main idea.

mcqs.q: Why does a paragraph keep ideas together?
options: So they are easy to read and understand
So they can become a poem
So they can join two words
So they can fill a speech bubble
mcqs.why: A paragraph keeps ideas together so that they are easy to read and understand for the reader.

mcqs.q: Where does a new paragraph start?
options: In the middle of a line
mcqs.why: The notes state clearly that a new paragraph starts on a new line in the writing.

mcqs.q: Which is the larger part: a chapter or a paragraph inside it?
options: A chapter is larger, and paragraphs live inside it
Both are exactly the same size
Neither is part of a book
mcqs.why: A chapter is a larger section of a book, and a paragraph is a smaller part that lives inside a chapter.

lessons.title: Oral Communication Skills — Ahmed talks to different people, changing his tone, words, and expressions accordingly (p. 126-127)
lessons.notes_html: 1. (Ahmed Talking to Teacher) Teacher: Ahmed, did you complete your homework? Ahmed: (politely, in a clear voice) Yes, Ma'am, I finished all my work. May I show it to you now? Teacher: Good job, Ahmed. Keep up the hard work. Ahmed: (smiling) Thank you, Ma'am. (Ahmed stands straight, uses respectful words, and nods while listening to the teacher.) 2. (Ahmed Talking to Friend) Ali: Hey Ahmed, let's play cricket. Ahmed: (excitedly, in a casual tone) Yes, let's go. I will bat first, and you will bowl, okay? Ali: Alright, but no cheating. Ahmed: (laughing) Don't worry, I'll play fair. (Ahmed uses a friendly tone, and smiles.) 3. (Ahmed Talking to Grandfather) Grandfather: Ahmed, my son, how was your day at school? Ahmed: (respectfully, in a soft tone) It was good, Dada Abu. I learned a new story in class. Would you like me to tell you? Grandfather: Yes, my son, I would love to hear it. (Ahmed sits politely, maintains eye contact, and tells the story slowly so that Grandfather can hear clearly.)

mcqs.q: How does Ahmed speak to his teacher?
mcqs.why: Ahmed speaks politely in a clear voice to his teacher, saying he finished all his work.

mcqs.q: What does Ahmed say to his teacher about his homework?
options: Yes, Ma'am, I finished all my work. May I show it to you now?
Dada Abu, I learned a story
mcqs.why: Ahmed politely tells his teacher, 'Yes, Ma'am, I finished all my work. May I show it to you now?'

mcqs.q: How does Ahmed behave while listening to his teacher?
options: He stands straight, uses respectful words, and nods while listening
He sits and avoids eye contact
He speaks in a casual tone
mcqs.why: With his teacher Ahmed stands straight, uses respectful words, and nods while listening to her.

mcqs.q: How does Ahmed speak to his friend Ali?
mcqs.why: Ahmed speaks excitedly in a casual tone to his friend Ali when they plan to play cricket.

mcqs.q: What game do Ahmed and Ali plan to play?
mcqs.why: Ali says, 'Hey Ahmed, let's play cricket,' and Ahmed agrees excitedly in a casual tone.

mcqs.q: What does Ahmed say he will do in the cricket game?
options: He will bat first, and Ali will bowl
He will keep the score only
mcqs.why: Ahmed says, 'I will bat first, and you will bowl, okay?' in his excited talk with Ali.

mcqs.q: What does Ahmed tell Ali about cheating?
options: You may cheat if you like
mcqs.why: Ahmed laughs and tells Ali, 'Don't worry, I'll play fair,' showing a friendly tone with his friend.

mcqs.q: How does Ahmed speak to his grandfather?
mcqs.why: Ahmed speaks respectfully in a soft tone to his grandfather, calling him Dada Abu politely.

mcqs.q: What does Ahmed offer to tell his grandfather?
options: A new story he learned in class
mcqs.why: Ahmed tells Dada Abu he learned a new story in class and asks if he would like to hear it.

mcqs.q: How does Ahmed tell the story to his grandfather?
options: Slowly, sitting politely and maintaining eye contact, so Grandfather can hear clearly
mcqs.why: Ahmed sits politely, maintains eye contact, and tells the story slowly so Grandfather can hear clearly.

lessons.title: Vocabulary — Compound Words (p. 127-128)
lessons.notes_html: Compound words are formed by combining two or more words to create a new word with a different meaning. 1. Noun + Noun -> Compound word. Examples: foot + ball = football; tooth + brush = toothbrush; school + bus = schoolbus. 2. Adjective + Noun -> Compound word. Examples: green + house = greenhouse; blue + berry = blueberry; black + board = blackboard.

mcqs.q: What are compound words?
options: Words formed by combining two or more words to create a new word with a different meaning
Words that join two sentences together
mcqs.why: Compound words are formed by combining two or more words to create a new word with a different meaning.

mcqs.q: Which combination makes 'football'?
options: Foot + ball, which is noun + noun
Green + house, which is adjective + noun
Blue + berry, which is adjective + noun
Black + board, which is adjective + noun
mcqs.why: Football is given as a noun + noun example, made by combining foot and ball into one word.

mcqs.q: Toothbrush is made from which two words?
mcqs.why: Toothbrush is a noun + noun compound word made from the two words tooth and brush.

mcqs.q: Schoolbus is an example of which type of compound word?
mcqs.why: Schoolbus, from school + bus, is listed under the noun + noun type of compound words.

mcqs.q: Which combination makes 'greenhouse'?
options: Green + house, which is adjective + noun
Foot + ball, which is noun + noun
Tooth + brush, which is noun + noun
School + bus, which is noun + noun
mcqs.why: Greenhouse is an adjective + noun compound word made by combining green and house.

mcqs.q: Blueberry is made from which two words?
mcqs.why: Blueberry is listed as an adjective + noun compound word made from blue and berry.

mcqs.q: Blackboard is an example of which type of compound word?
mcqs.why: Blackboard, from black + board, is given under the adjective + noun type of compound words.

mcqs.q: In 'blackboard', the word 'black' is:
mcqs.why: Black describes the board, so in the adjective + noun pattern, black is the adjective part.

mcqs.q: In 'toothbrush', both 'tooth' and 'brush' are:
mcqs.why: Toothbrush follows the noun + noun pattern, so both tooth and brush are nouns in this example.

mcqs.q: A compound word has a meaning that is:
options: Exactly the same as one small word
A different meaning from the words alone
mcqs.why: The definition says combining words creates a new word with a different meaning from the parts.

lessons.title: Grammar — Joining words (p. 129-130)
lessons.notes_html:
Joining words are used to connect words, phrases, clauses, or sentences. Function of Joining Words in Sentences: 'and' - 1. She likes to read mystery novels and watch detective shows. 2. He enjoys playing basketball and soccer in his free time. 3. The restaurant serves pizza and pasta. 'or' - 1. Would you like tea or juice for breakfast? 2. You can choose to go to the park or stay home. 3. Do you prefer to sit by the window or middle seat of the bus? 'but' - 1. She studied hard for the exam, but she still didn't get a good grade. 2. He wanted to go to the

party, but he had to finish his homework. 3. The weather forecast predicted sunshine, but it ended up raining all day.

mcqs.q: What are joining words used to connect?
options: Only two pictures in a book
Only the parts of a compound word
Only the steps of a recipe
mcqs.why: Joining words are used to connect words, phrases, clauses, or sentences, as the grammar lesson states.

mcqs.q: In 'She likes to read mystery novels and watch detective shows', the joining word is:
mcqs.why: The word 'and' joins the two activities of reading mystery novels and watching detective shows.

mcqs.q: Which sentence uses 'and' as a joining word?
options: Would you like tea or juice?
The restaurant serves pizza and pasta.
She studied hard, but she didn't get a good grade.
Do you prefer the window seat?
mcqs.why: The sentence about the restaurant serving pizza and pasta uses 'and' to join the two foods.

mcqs.q: In 'Would you like tea or juice for breakfast?', the joining word is:
mcqs.why: The word 'or' joins the two choices, tea and juice, offered for breakfast in this sentence.

mcqs.q: Which sentence uses 'or' as a joining word?
options: He enjoys playing basketball and soccer.
You can choose to go to the park or stay home.
The forecast predicted sunshine, but it rained.
She likes mystery novels and detective shows.
mcqs.why: The sentence about choosing to go to the park or stay home uses 'or' to join the two choices.

mcqs.q: In 'Do you prefer to sit by the window or middle seat of the bus?', 'or' joins:
mcqs.why: Here 'or' joins two choices of seat on the bus: by the window or the middle seat.

mcqs.q: In 'She studied hard for the exam, but she still didn't get a good grade', the joining word is:
mcqs.why: The word 'but' joins the two parts and shows the contrast in this exam sentence.

mcqs.q: Which sentence uses 'but' as a joining word?
options: The restaurant serves pizza and pasta.
Would you like tea or juice?
He wanted to go to the party, but he had to finish his homework.
She enjoys hiking as well as swimming.
mcqs.why: The party sentence uses 'but' because he wanted to go but had to finish his homework first.

mcqs.q: What happened in the weather sentence with 'but'?
options: The forecast predicted sunshine, but it ended up raining all day
The forecast predicted rain and it rained
The weather stayed sunny all day
The forecast was about a bus seat
mcqs.why: The example says the forecast predicted sunshine, but it ended up raining all day instead.

mcqs.q: He enjoys playing which two games in the 'and' example?
mcqs.why: The 'and' example says he enjoys playing basketball and soccer in his free time.

lessons.title: Use of Simple Connectors (p. 130-131)
lessons.notes_html: 1. For Addition: 'and' - He likes to read novels and stories. 'as well as' - She enjoys hiking as well as swimming. 2. For Reason: 'because' - He didn't go to work because he was sick. 'since' - She stayed indoors since it was raining. 3. For Sequence: 'first, second, third' - First, we need to gather the ingredients. Second, we'll mix them together. Third, we will bake the mixture in the oven.

mcqs.why: The lesson lists 'and' and 'as well as' as the simple connectors used for addition.

mcqs.q: In 'He likes to read novels and stories', the connector 'and' is used for:
mcqs.why: The connector 'and' adds stories to novels, so it is used for addition in this example sentence.

mcqs.q: In 'She enjoys hiking as well as swimming', 'as well as' is used for:
mcqs.why: The connector 'as well as' adds swimming to hiking, so it is used for addition in this example.

mcqs.q: Which connector is used for reason in 'He didn't go to work because he was sick'?
mcqs.why: The connector 'because' gives the reason he did not go to work: he was sick that day.

mcqs.q: Which connectors are used for reason?
mcqs.why: The lesson lists 'because' and 'since' as the connectors used for reason in sentences.

mcqs.q: In 'She stayed indoors since it was raining', 'since' gives:
mcqs.why: The connector 'since' gives the reason she stayed indoors, which was that it was raining.

mcqs.q: Which words are used for sequence?
mcqs.why: The lesson lists 'first, second, third' as the words used to show sequence in a procedure.

mcqs.q: In the sequence example, what is done first?
options: We bake the mixture in the oven
We serve the food on a plate
mcqs.why: The sequence example says first we need to gather the ingredients before mixing and baking them.

options: We bake the mixture in the oven
mcqs.why: The sequence example says second we will mix them together, after gathering the ingredients first.

mcqs.q: In the sequence example, what is done third?
options: We bake the mixture in the oven
mcqs.why: The sequence example says third we will bake the mixture in the oven, completing the steps.

lessons.title: Writing B — Write a recipe for making an omelette (p. 132)

lessons.title: Fact, Fiction and Non-Fiction (p. 136-137)
lessons.notes_html:
Fact: A fact is a statement that can be proven to be true or false through evidence or observation. Example: The Earth orbits the Sun. This is a fact because it can be confirmed through scientific observation and research. Fictional Text: Fictional text refers to written works that present imagined or invented stories, characters, and events. Non-fiction Texts: Non-fictional text refers to written works that present factual information, real events, and actual experiences. Types of Fictional and Non-Fictional Texts: Fictional Texts - Fictional texts are stories that are made up from someone's imagination. They are not real. Here are three common types: 1. Novels: Example: Harry Potter and the Sorcerer's Stone, is a long story with many characters and chapters that follow Harry's magical journey. 2. Short Stories: Example: The Thirsty Crow is a short story with a beginning, middle, and end, that focuses on one main event. 3. Fairy Tales: Example: Cinderella is a magical story of a kind girl. Non-Fictional Texts - Non-fictional texts are books or articles that are about real people, real places, or real things. Here are three important types: 1. Biographies: Example: The Story of Abdul Sattar Edhi is a book that talks about the life and work of a real person. 2. Informational Texts: Example: A book about plants gives scientific facts, has pictures, diagrams, and headings. 3. News Articles: Example: A newspaper report about a school event tells what happened, where, when, and includes quotes from

people.

lessons.title: Poetic Devices (p. 138-139)
lessons.notes_html: Poetic devices are special tricks that poets use to make poems more fun to read and listen to. Read the Poem aloud: 'A Walk in the Garden' (Edited for Clarity) - I walk in the garden at the break of day, / Birds are singing in a cheerful way. / Flowers bloom in red and blue, / The sky above is bright and true. / I walk, I walk, I walk some more, / Past the tree and by the door. / The sun is like a golden ball, / Shining gently over all. Poetic devices in the Poem: 1. Rhyme and Rhythm - Rhyme is when words at the end of a line sound the same. Rhythm is the beat of the poem. Examples: day / way; blue / true; more / door; ball / all. 2. Repetition - Repetition is when a word or a line is repeated. Examples: 'I walk, I walk, I walk some more'. 3. Simile - A simile compares two different things using the words 'like' or 'as'. Examples: 'The sun is like a golden ball'. 4. Sensory Images - Sensory images are words that help us see, hear, smell, or feel things in the poem. Examples: Hear: 'Birds are singing'; See: 'Flowers bloom in red and blue'; 'The sun is like a golden ball'.
